rendered:
The paper does not report any measured amount of nickel, manganese or cobalt leaching into the Cyrene. It states the opposite: the relative ratios of those metals stayed the same, so the separation process does not leach them. The NMC622 ratios were consistent before and after separation, which the paper says shows the process does not leach the transition metals. The paper says the ICP-OES results confirm this, but those results are in its supplementary Table S1, which is not part of this document.[1][2][3]

The leaching the paper does discuss is lithium, not nickel, manganese or cobalt. It says the lithium leaching from NMC622 occurred after recovery. The paper attributes this to the ether groups in Cyrene: the molecule has two ether groups[4], which attract lithium cations because ether is electron-donating. That attraction causes lithium leaching and makes the high-Ni cathode less stable.[5][6][7]

Later, the paper attributes the electrochemical degradation of the recovered NMC622 to both this lithium leaching and possible surface changes caused by the Cyrene solvent.[8]
